message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review was carried out rigorously and, importantly, independently: the contractor's delay analysis was tested and agreed by our independent project manager, so the allocation of the 70 days of delay is not just the contractor's version. The findings are clear. The single biggest cause was the unforeseen ground conditions, which trace back to a thin site investigation, and the recommendation on full-footprint investigations addresses that head on. The commercial position is equally clear: the contractor carries 14 days, so we recover £45,000 in liquidated damages, and the overrun is explained by identifiable causes. The review also looks beyond this one project. By comparing all our education projects since 2022, we found that two-stage tendering is associated with delays a third as long as single-stage, which gives us an evidence-based case for changing our default procurement route. Every recommendation is specific and actionable. I believe the review gives Members a fair, well-documented account and a sound basis for improving future projects.
</author>

<document>
Project Review: Delay to Practical Completion, Riverside Primary School Extension
Capital Projects Team, Mereford Council, November 2026

1. Purpose
This review explains why the Riverside Primary School extension reached practical completion ten weeks late, sets out the commercial position with the contractor, and draws lessons for the Council's capital programme.

2. Project summary
The project added a four-classroom teaching block and a new hall to Riverside Primary School. The contract was let on a single-stage design and build basis to Hartwell Construction in November 2025, with a contract sum of £3.84 million and a planned practical completion date of 14 August 2026, so that the new block would be ready for the September intake. Practical completion was certified on 23 October 2026, 70 days late. Pupils were accommodated in temporary classrooms for the first half of the autumn term.

3. Causes of delay
The contractor's delay analysis was reviewed by the Council's independent project manager, who agreed the following allocation of critical-path delay.

Table 1. Critical-path delay by cause
Cause | Days of delay | Responsibility under the contract
Unforeseen ground conditions (old foundations found during excavation) | 21 | Council (relevant event)
Late design changes requested by the school (extra fit-out to two classrooms) | 28 | Council (relevant event)
Delayed delivery of structural steel | 14 | Contractor
Exceptionally wet weather beyond the contract allowance | 7 | Neutral (time but no money)
Total | 70 |

The largest single cause of delay was the unforeseen ground conditions. The site investigation commissioned at feasibility stage used only four trial pits, none of which was located in the footprint of the new hall, where the old foundations were found.

The late design changes arose because the school's requirements for the two classrooms changed after the contract was signed, when the school decided to use them as a specialist resource base. The steel delay arose from the supplier's mill schedule, and the contractor did not identify an alternative supplier.

4. Commercial position
The contract provides for liquidated damages of £2,500 for each day of delay for which the contractor is responsible. The contractor is responsible for 14 days, so the Council will deduct £45,000 in liquidated damages from the final account. The contractor is entitled to an extension of time, but not to additional payment, for the 7 days of exceptional weather.

The final account has been agreed at £4.21 million, an overrun of £370,000 (9.6%) on the contract sum, mainly due to the ground works and the design changes.

5. Comparison with other projects
We compared Riverside with the Council's other education capital projects completed since 2022. The six projects let on a two-stage tender basis finished on average three weeks late, while the five let on a single-stage basis, including Riverside, finished on average nine weeks late. Two-stage tendering therefore reduces delay, and the Council should adopt it as the default procurement route for education projects. The two-stage projects were all refurbishments of existing buildings with budgets under £1.5 million; the single-stage projects were all new-build extensions.

6. Lessons and recommendations
6.1 Adopt two-stage tendering as the default for education capital projects over £1 million.
6.2 Require site investigations to cover the full footprint of any new building, with trial pits or boreholes at each proposed foundation zone.
6.3 Freeze client requirements at contract signature, with any later changes approved by the Director of Education and costed for time and money before instruction.
6.4 Require contractors to identify alternative suppliers for long-lead structural items at tender stage.

7. Conclusion
The delay at Riverside was caused principally by unforeseen ground conditions arising from an inadequate site investigation, compounded by steel supply problems and late changes. Adopting two-stage tendering, together with the specific measures above, would reduce the risk of a recurrence on future projects.
</document>
response:
# Review: Riverside Primary School Extension Delay Report

The report is well structured, and the delay table, cost figures and three of the four recommendations are clear and useful. However, it has two factual errors that would be embarrassing in front of Members, and one finding is not supported by the evidence. These need fixing before it goes out.

## Must fix

**1. The ground conditions were not the largest cause of delay.**
Your own Table 1 shows late design changes caused **28 days** and ground conditions **21 days**. So "the largest single cause of delay was the unforeseen ground conditions" (Section 3) is wrong. The conclusion repeats the error ("caused principally by unforeseen ground conditions… compounded by… late changes").

This matters beyond accuracy. The biggest cause was the Council's own client-side change, made after contract signature. Presenting it as a secondary factor understates the governance lesson, and a reader checking the table will notice.

Suggested fix: lead with the design changes in both Section 3 and Section 7. Point out that the two Council-side causes together account for 49 of the 70 days (70%).

**2. The liquidated damages figure is wrong.**
14 days × £2,500 = **£35,000**, not £45,000. This figure goes into the final account and to Members, so check where £45,000 came from. Is it an arithmetic slip, a different LD rate, or a different number of days? Then correct it throughout.

**3. The two-stage tendering finding is not supported, and Recommendation 6.1 rests on it.**
Section 5 states that two-stage tendering "reduces delay." But the paragraph itself says the two groups differ in more than procurement route:
- All six two-stage projects were **refurbishments under £1.5m**.
- All five single-stage projects were **new-build extensions**.

Project type, scale and procurement route are completely confounded. The 3-week vs 9-week difference could be explained entirely by new builds being larger and carrying more ground and design risk. The data cannot separate the effect of the procurement route from the others. With 11 projects, it couldn't do so robustly even if the groups were matched.

There are two further problems:
- **The threshold doesn't match the evidence.** Recommendation 6.1 applies to projects over £1m. The two-stage evidence comes only from refurbishments under £1.5m, and it includes no new builds at all.
- **It doesn't follow from this project's causes.** The Riverside delays came from a thin site investigation, a post-contract change in client requirements, and a steel supply problem. Recommendations 6.2–6.4 address these directly. The report doesn't explain how two-stage tendering would have prevented any of them. There is an arguable case, since early contractor involvement can surface ground and buildability risk, but the report needs to make it.

Suggested fix: either remove 6.1, or recast Section 5 as an observation. For example: "Two-stage projects in our portfolio have finished closer to programme, but these were all smaller refurbishments, so we cannot attribute the difference to procurement route. We recommend piloting two-stage tendering on the next new-build education project over £1m and comparing outcomes." Remove the two-stage reference from the conclusion as well.

## Should address

**4. Concurrency of delays.** The four causes add up to exactly 70 days, which implies they ran one after another on the critical path. If the steel delay overlapped with either Council-caused delay, the contractor may dispute the 14 days and so the LDs. Add one sentence confirming that the project manager considered concurrency. This strengthens the commercial position.

**5. How independent the review is.** The project manager is independent of the contractor, but that is different from the review being independent. If the same project manager administered the contract, they may have been involved in decisions under review, such as the site investigation scope or instructing the design changes. Say who the project manager is and what their role was, so Members can judge this themselves.

**6. Cost breakdown.** "Mainly due to the ground works and the design changes" is too vague for a £370,000 overrun. Split it into:
- ground works
- design changes
- loss and expense or prolongation for the 49 Council-caused days (the contractor is presumably entitled to this)
- any other items

Also state whether the cost of the temporary classrooms is included. If it isn't, the true cost to the Council is understated.

**7. The design change decision.** Recommendation 6.3 is good. The report would be stronger if it briefly explained why the resource-base decision came after contract signature, and whether anyone weighed the time and cost impact before the change was instructed.

## Checked and correct
- 70 days = 10 weeks; 14 August → 23 October 2026 is 70 days.
- £4.21m − £3.84m = £370,000, which is 9.6% of the contract sum.
- The weather is correctly treated as an extension of time without additional payment.
- Recommendations 6.2–6.4 are specific and tied to identified causes.

## On your summary
Most of your description holds up, but three points don't:
- The ground conditions were not the biggest cause.
- The LDs are £35,000, not £45,000.
- The comparison shows two-stage projects *were associated with* shorter delays. It does not provide an evidence-based case for changing the default route, because project type and size explain the gap at least as well.

With those fixed, the report would give Members a fair and well-documented account.
